flashcards.q: Storage classes with minimum durations and retrieval costs?
flashcards.a: Standard (no min, no retrieval fee), Nearline (30d min, ~$0.01/GB retrieval), Coldline (90d min, ~$0.02/GB), Archive (365d min, ~$0.05/GB). All share one API and ms latency - early deletion pays remaining days.

Per-object on get-method access: >=128KiB objects unaccessed 30 days move toward Nearline (default terminal); with Archive terminal: 90d -> Coldline, 365d -> Archive; any access moves back to Standard. Management fee but retrieval/early-deletion fees waived.
Strong global read-after-write since 2010: once a write returns, all readers everywhere see it, including listings. No cross-object atomicity though.

Hardware clocks (GPS + atomic) bound clock uncertainty to interval [earliest, latest], eps typically low-single-digit ms, worst-case bound ~7ms. commit_ts = TT.now().latest. Commit-wait until TT.now().earliest > commit_ts before ack.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't commit-wait add 7ms to every write?
flashcards.a: The wait runs in parallel with Paxos quorum replication round-trips; only when quorum finishes faster than the uncertainty window does residual wait exist. Bounded worst case, not constant overhead.

External/strict serializability = serial order matches real-time commit order observable anywhere globally. Spanner guarantees it via TrueTime+commit-wait; ordinary serializable systems (e.g., CockroachDB with HLC) don't promise real-time ordering across nodes.

CRDB uses hybrid logical clocks on commodity hardware: serializable + snapshot reads, but wall-clock-later transactions can receive earlier timestamps across nodes (new-enemy anomaly class). Spanner's hardware-bounded uncertainty eliminates that gap.

More than 4x transactional throughput and up to 100x analytical query speedup versus standard PostgreSQL per Google's tests - via disaggregated log-structured storage plus an in-memory columnar engine (HTAP without ETL). Benchmarks, not contracts.

flashcards.q: Why do writes hot-spot one node and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: Monotonic key prefixes (timestamps, sequential IDs) route to a single tablet. Fix at schema time: hash/reverse high-cardinality components, salt prefixes, pad IDs. Adding nodes doesn't help - the bottleneck is one tablet.

Index-driven queries only: no joins, limited aggregations; ~1MiB doc cap; per-operation pricing makes N+1 reads and chatty listeners budget killers. Great for per-user document state with offline sync; wrong for relational or analytics-heavy shapes.

flashcards.q: When does Cloud SQL stop being enough?
flashcards.a: Vertical scale ceilings, storage-layer I/O bottlenecks, read-replica lag, or analytics needing ETL out. AlloyDB answers with bigger shapes, read pool (1-20 nodes ~), columnar HTAP, ScaNN vectors - same PostgreSQL wire protocol.
Local reads ~5ms (~), cross-zone commits tens of ms (~50-100ms p99 ~), multi-region higher. Reads can use bounded-staleness snapshot timestamps for lock-free consistent reads from any replica.
